title: Calling other services: REST, RPC and gRPC
goal: By the end you can explain why a remote call is not a local call, compare REST with OpenAPI and gRPC with deadlines, say why one gRPC connection defeats an L4 load balancer, and write a client whose retries can't charge a card twice.

warmup.q: Your checkout service calls `POST /charges` on the payment service with a 2-second timeout. The timeout fires. What do you know about the charge?
options: It failed: the payment service never got the request
It went through, but the reply was slow
Nothing: it may have failed, gone through, or still be running
It was rolled back, because the client hung up
warmup.why: A timeout only says no reply arrived in time. The request may have been lost, the card may have been charged with the reply lost, or the server may still be working. Nothing rolls a charge back when a client stops waiting. The first option is the tempting one, because it is what a failed local call would mean.

sections.h: A remote call can end in a way a local call can't
sections.body:
A local function call takes about a nanosecond. The Try below times one small `authorize` function three ways on a laptop. Called directly, it takes about 1 ns. Called through gRPC inside the same JVM, about 10 µs. Called through gRPC over TCP on 127.0.0.1, about 75 µs, and that is with no real network in the way. Between two machines in one datacenter a round trip costs a few hundred microseconds; between two regions, about 70 ms.

People have tried to hide that gap for forty years. Andrew Birrell and Bruce Nelson's 1984 paper on **remote procedure calls** (RPC) set the goal: a call to another machine should look exactly like a call to a local procedure. That goal is called location transparency, and Java RMI, CORBA, Enterprise JavaBeans and SOAP all chased it. In 1994 Jim Waldo and three colleagues at Sun Microsystems wrote "A Note on Distributed Computing" to say the goal was wrong. They named four differences no stub can hide. Latency: four to five orders of magnitude, they wrote, and likely to grow. Memory access: a pointer means nothing in another process. Partial failure. And concurrency. Around the same time L. Peter Deutsch, also at Sun, listed the fallacies of distributed computing, beliefs that every new distributed program quietly assumes: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology doesn't change, there is one administrator, and transport cost is zero. James Gosling added an eighth around 1997: the network is homogeneous.

Partial failure is the one that bites payment code. A local call ends in one of three ways: it returns, it throws, or the process dies and takes the caller with it. A remote call has a fourth ending. Your checkout service sends `Charge(pay-1, 40.00 EUR)` to the payment service and waits 300 ms. Nothing comes back. Maybe the request was lost and nothing happened. Maybe the payment service charged the card and the reply was lost. Maybe it is still working. To the client all three look the same, a timeout, and waiting longer doesn't settle it.

Keep this picture for the whole lesson: a request goes out, work happens, a reply comes back, and any of the three can go missing. REST and gRPC are two ways to write down what travels. Deadlines decide how long to wait. Load balancers and service discovery decide where the request lands. Idempotency keys make it safe to ask again. The stepper walks through the endings.

try.title: Time a local call against a remote one
steps: Open `CallCostDemo.kt`. It times the same `authorize` function three ways: a direct call, gRPC over the in-process transport (the whole gRPC stack without a socket), and gRPC over HTTP/2 on 127.0.0.1.
Predict the ratio between the direct call and the loopback gRPC call: 10, 1,000 or 100,000?
Run it from the `labs` folder with the command below. It takes about 5 seconds.

code.title: CallCostDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
local function call              about 1.1 ns per call
gRPC, in-process transport       median    10.96 us   p99    29.00 us
gRPC, HTTP/2 over 127.0.0.1      median    76.71 us   p99   197.92 us
```
Numbers vary with the machine and how busy it is (this run: an Apple laptop, JDK 25), but the ratios hold. About 1 ns against about 75 µs is a factor of about 70,000, close to Waldo's five orders of magnitude, without any real network. The in-process line is the cost of gRPC itself: encoding, the call machinery and a hand-off between threads. The p99 column shows the other thing a remote call does: its time varies, here by more than 2 times between the median and the slowest 1%.

sections.h: REST: resources, HTTP methods and a contract you can check
sections.body:
REST comes from Roy Fielding's 2000 dissertation. It treats an API as a set of resources, each named by a URL, that clients act on with HTTP's few methods. A payments API might have `POST /v1/charges` to create a charge, `GET /v1/charges/ch_77` to read one, and `POST /v1/charges/ch_77/refunds` to refund it. Bodies are usually JSON. Everything else comes from HTTP itself: status codes (`201 Created`, `404 Not Found`, `409 Conflict`), caching for GETs, authentication headers. Fielding's definition also asks for hypertext (responses that carry links to the next actions), which most APIs called REST skip. In practice "REST" means resource URLs, HTTP methods and JSON.

Part of REST's appeal is that it doesn't pretend to be a function call. A request is a message about a resource, and HTTP already says which methods are safe to repeat: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST isn't (the Networking track's lesson on retries).

**OpenAPI** writes the contract down: a YAML or JSON file with every path, parameter, request and response schema, and status code. Version 3.2.0 came out in September 2025, and 3.2.1 in September 2026. From that file, tools generate client libraries, server stubs and documentation. Some teams write the file first and generate code from it (contract-first); others annotate their code and generate the file (code-first). Either way, CI can compare the new file with the last released one and fail the build on a breaking change.

What counts as breaking follows from the deploy order. You deploy the server first, then the clients, which can take months for a mobile app and forever for a partner's integration. So the new server must read old clients' requests (backward compatibility for requests), and old clients must read the new server's responses (forward compatibility for responses): the rules of lesson 2 of this track, applied to an API. Adding an optional request field or a response field is safe, as long as clients ignore fields they don't know. Removing, renaming or retyping a field breaks someone.

When a break can't be avoided, the API needs versions. The usual answer is `/v1/` then `/v2/` in the URL, which forks the server code, and old clients never move. Stripe gives every breaking change a dated version instead. An account is pinned to the version current at its first request, and a `Stripe-Version` header can override the pin for one request. Stripe's 2017 write-up explains the trick: the server builds each response at the newest version, then runs it back through small "version change" modules until it has the shape the caller's version expects. Since `2024-09-30.acacia`, Stripe ships a non-breaking release every month and allows breaking changes only in two named major releases a year. The newest as of November 2026 is `2026-10-28.endive`.

sections.h: gRPC: a Protobuf contract on HTTP/2, with a deadline on every call

try.title: Follow one deadline through two services
steps: Open `DeadlineDemo.kt`. Checkout calls payments with a 300 ms deadline. Payments works for 120 ms, then calls the issuer and sets no deadline of its own. The issuer needs 500 ms.
Predict how much time the issuer sees left when its call arrives, and who gives up first.
Run it.

code.title: DeadlineDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
   0 ms  checkout calls payments with a 300 ms deadline
   1 ms  payments got pay-1, 299 ms left
 127 ms  issuer   got pay-1, 173 ms left
 311 ms  checkout gets DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
 312 ms  payments issuer call ended: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
 321 ms  issuer   sees the call cancelled, stops
```
Payments never set a deadline, yet the issuer saw 173 ms left: grpc-java passed on what remained of checkout's 300 ms. At about 310 ms all three give up together. Without that, the issuer would have spent its full 500 ms on an answer nobody was waiting for, while holding a thread. Timings vary by a few milliseconds.

sections.h: One connection, one backend: balancing gRPC and finding services
sections.body:
The Networking track's lesson on load balancers drew the line: an L4 balancer picks a backend when a TCP connection opens and then just copies bytes, while an L7 balancer reads each request and picks a backend for each one. HTTP/1.1 clients blur the difference, because a pool of 20 connections spreads over up to 20 backends. gRPC exposes it. A gRPC channel opens one HTTP/2 connection to an address and runs every call over it as a separate stream, for as long as the connection lives. Put an L4 balancer in front of three replicas, and the channel's one connection lands on one replica, and every call follows. In the Try below, 300 calls through an L4 proxy arrive as 300, 0 and 0. Three channels give 100 each, but only because each opened its own connection.

Kubernetes makes this the default trap. An ordinary Service has one virtual IP, and kube-proxy balances connections to it at L4, so a client's gRPC traffic ends up pinned to one pod. Pods that an autoscaler adds get almost nothing until clients reconnect.

There are three ways out. First, an L7 proxy that understands HTTP/2 and balances each stream: Envoy, or a service mesh such as Linkerd or Istio, which runs a proxy next to every pod. Second, balancing in the client: the client learns every replica's address and spreads its calls itself. grpc-java's `round_robin` policy does that, and a headless Kubernetes Service (`clusterIP: None`) makes DNS return every pod's IP instead of one virtual IP. Third, as a stopgap, servers can cap connection age (`NettyServerBuilder.maxConnectionAge`), so clients reconnect every few minutes and get spread again.

The second fix raises a question every service has anyway: how does a client learn the addresses? This is **service discovery**, and it has its own ladder. A hard-coded address breaks when the server moves. DNS with several records works, but every cache keeps a dead address until its TTL runs out (the Networking track's lesson on DNS). A registry such as etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul tracks live instances: each instance registers its address and sends heartbeats, and clients query or watch the registry. Kubernetes keeps that registry for you as each Service's endpoints. A mesh hides the whole question from your code, at the price of an extra proxy on every request's path.

try.title: 300 calls, three replicas, three ways
steps: Open `BalancingDemo.kt`. It starts three replicas on 127.0.0.1, a small L4 proxy that picks a replica for each new TCP connection, and a name resolver that returns all three addresses, the way DNS does for a headless Service.
Predict the three counts for each line before you run it.
Run it.

code.title: BalancingDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
one channel through the L4 proxy       replica-1=300  replica-2=0  replica-3=0
three channels through the L4 proxy    replica-1=100  replica-2=100  replica-3=100
one channel, client-side round_robin   replica-1=99  replica-2=102  replica-3=99
```
The proxy chose a replica once per connection, so one channel meant one replica. Three channels spread out only because they made three connections. With `round_robin` the client holds a connection to every replica and picks one per call. The counts are about 100, not exactly 100, because the first calls go out while the other connections are still opening.

sections.h: A retry is safe only with an idempotency key
sections.body:
Back to the fourth ending. Checkout got `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` for `pay-1`, and it has two choices. The Try below counts both over 1,000 payments in which 30% of first replies are lost after the card was charged. If checkout gives up, 313 payments are reported as failed although every card was charged, and someone reconciles them by hand. If it retries, every payment succeeds and 313 cards are charged twice. gRPC's own retry policy has the same problem: it resends the request, and the server can't tell a retry from a new payment.

The fix is to make the retry recognizable. The client makes up one **idempotency key** per logical operation, usually a random UUID, before the first attempt, and sends the same key with every attempt. The server claims the key atomically before doing any work, stores the result under it, and answers every later request with that key from the store. The Caching track's lesson on idempotency keys built that store in Redis. This lesson adds the client's side and the rules that make it work end to end.

Stripe's API (v1) has the best-known rules. The client generates the key, up to 255 characters. Stripe saves the status code and body of the first request once its execution begins, even a 500 error, and replays them for any retry with that key. Keys can be pruned once they are at least 24 hours old, so a retry after that is a new request. Reusing a key with different parameters is rejected with an error. A request that fails validation, or collides with a request still running under the same key, isn't saved, so it can be retried. Every POST accepts a key; on GET and DELETE, which are idempotent already, a key has no effect. (Stripe's v2 API changes one rule: a retry drives a failed request to completion instead of replaying the stored error.) The IETF is standardizing an `Idempotency-Key` HTTP header; its draft reached revision 08 in October 2026 and is not yet an RFC.

Three mistakes break keys in practice. A key made per attempt instead of per payment protects nothing; in the Try, that row is exactly as bad as no key. A key stored after the work instead of claimed before it lets two concurrent attempts both charge, and that is the common case, because a retry after a timeout arrives while the slow first attempt is still running. And a key that stops at your service protects only your service. When the payment service calls the card issuer, it must send a key of its own, derived from the client's (`k-7f/issuer`), or a crash between the issuer's answer and your database commit charges the card twice anyway. Lesson 5 of this track meets the same rule inside a workflow engine.

In gRPC, put the key in the request message, like field 3 of `ChargeRequest` above. A metadata header also works, but a field is part of the contract: it shows in the `.proto`, it is logged with the request, and no proxy that rewrites headers can drop it.

try.title: Count duplicate charges for four kinds of client
steps: Open `RetryDuplicatesDemo.kt`. One server and four clients: no retries, retries without a key, retries with a fresh key per attempt, and retries with one key per payment. A seeded random picks the 30% of payments whose first reply is lost after the charge.
Predict the duplicates column for each row.
Run it.

code.title: RetryDuplicatesDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
client                      charges  duplicates  reported failed
no retry                       1000           0              313
retry no key                   1313         313                0
retry new key each time        1313         313                0
retry one key                  1000           0                0
```
313 payments were unlucky. Without retries, all 313 were charged and reported as failed: money taken, order not placed. Retrying without a key, or with a new key each time, fixes that and charges each of the 313 twice. Only one key per payment, sent on every attempt, gives 1,000 charges and no failures.

refs.title: Brandur Leach: Implementing Stripe-like Idempotency Keys in Postgres (2017)
IETF draft: The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field

analogy: Calling another service is like sending a courier across town with a written order for a supplier. If the courier isn't back by five, you don't know whether the order got there, whether the supplier filled it, or whether the courier is stuck in traffic with the receipt in their pocket. Send a second courier with a copy and you may get two deliveries. So you write an order number at the top, and the supplier's clerk checks the order book: if number 7f is already in it, they hand over a copy of the same receipt. The analogy breaks at the clerk. A person might notice that two orders look alike; a server sees only bytes, so it can spot a repeat only by a key the client chose to send, and only for as long as it remembers that key.
in_your_world: Your Quarkus services call card issuers over HTTP and each other over REST or gRPC. Three checks are worth doing this week. Does every outgoing call have a deadline, shorter than what is left of the request that caused it? Does every retry, whether your own loop, a MicroProfile `@Retry` from SmallRye Fault Tolerance or a gRPC retry policy, resend only requests that carry an idempotency key made once per payment? And if your gRPC services run on Kubernetes behind an ordinary ClusterIP Service, look at requests per pod: one busy pod and idle new ones is the pinned-connection signature, fixed by a headless Service with `round_robin` or by a mesh. When a Temporal activity calls the issuer, the key comes from the workflow ID, which the next lesson shows.
mistake: Turning on retries without keys. A team adds `@Retry(maxRetries = 3)` to the client for `POST /charges`, or a retry policy to the gRPC service config, because the network is flaky. Errors on the dashboard drop to zero, and a week later the reconciliation report shows duplicate charges. People make this mistake because a retry looks like a pure reliability fix, and the duplicates show up somewhere else, in another team's numbers. The fix: retry only failures that mean "didn't get through or don't know" (gRPC `UNAVAILABLE` and `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`; for HTTP, connection errors, 502, 503 and 504), only for requests that carry one key per operation, with a server that claims the key before doing the work, and at one layer only.

compare.title: The same charge as a REST call and as a gRPC call

a.label: REST over HTTP/1.1
a.title: request and response
a.src:
POST /v1/charges HTTP/1.1
Host: api.payments.example
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: 5f1c2a9e-8d43-4f2b-9b1e-7d0c3a6e2b41

{"payment_id":"pay-1","amount_cents":4000}

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":"ch_77","amount_cents":4000}

b.label: gRPC over HTTP/2
b.title: the frames, simplified
b.src:
HEADERS  :method POST   :path /payments.v1.Charges/Charge
         content-type application/grpc   grpc-timeout 300m
DATA     00 | 00 00 00 30 | 0a 05 70 61 79 2d 31 10 a0 1f 1a 24 ...
         flag | length 48 | field 1 "pay-1", field 2 4000, field 3 the key

HEADERS  :status 200   content-type application/grpc
DATA     00 | 00 00 00 0a | 0a 05 63 68 5f 37 37 10 a0 1f
HEADERS  grpc-status 0          (trailers: the real outcome)

compare.note: Both send the same charge with the same key. REST sends field names as JSON text, puts the key in a header and reports the outcome in the HTTP status line. gRPC sends 48 bytes of Protobuf with field numbers instead of names, each message after a 5-byte prefix, and the key is a field of the message. Its HTTP status is 200 even when the call fails: the outcome is `grpc-status` in the trailers, so a proxy that wants to count gRPC errors must read trailers. The deadline is a header the server can act on (`300m` is 300 milliseconds); plain HTTP has no standard way to tell the server how long the client will wait.

worked.title: Turn on gRPC's own retries, and see why the key still matters

steps.say: gRPC can retry for you. The policy lives in the channel's service config, a JSON-shaped map: which method, how many attempts in all (the first one counts), the backoff, and which status codes to retry. Retry only `UNAVAILABLE`, the code for "didn't get through".
steps.code:
val serviceConfig = mapOf(
    "methodConfig" to listOf(
        mapOf(
            "name" to listOf(mapOf("service" to "payments.v1.Charges", "method" to "Charge")),
            "retryPolicy" to mapOf(
                "maxAttempts" to 4.0, // the JSON numbers of a service config are doubles
                "initialBackoff" to "0.05s",
                "maxBackoff" to "1s",
                "backoffMultiplier" to 2.0,
                "retryableStatusCodes" to listOf("UNAVAILABLE"),
            ),
        ),
    ),
)

steps.say: Hand the config to the channel and switch retries on. (A name resolver can also supply a service config, so the service's owners can set the policy for all their clients.)

Set one deadline per call. Unlike the loop in the lab, which gives each attempt its own deadline, gRPC's policy retries inside the call's original deadline: all attempts together must finish in 2 seconds here. That is also why `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` is normally not on the retry list.

`RetryPolicyDemo.kt` runs this against a server that charges and then loses every other reply. Every call succeeds and the application never sees an error, but 5 payments made 10 charges. The policy did exactly what it was told. Add an idempotency key to the request and a key store on the server, and each second attempt becomes a replay.
steps.code:
$ ./gradlew :flow:demo -Pmain=sfz.enc.l04.demo.RetryPolicyDemoKt --console=plain -q
pay-0 -> ch_2
pay-1 -> ch_4
pay-2 -> ch_6
pay-3 -> ch_8
pay-4 -> ch_10
requests that arrived: 10, cards charged: 10 for 5 payments

lab.title: A gRPC client that retries safely, and the key store that makes it safe
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder. All 11 fail: five in `IdempotencyStoreTest` and six in `ChargeClientTest`. The client tests start a real gRPC server in the same JVM with the in-process transport, so there is no Docker and no port.

Read `ChargeRpc.kt` (the method descriptor and hand-written Protobuf marshallers, no code generation) and `ChargeServer.kt` (the issuer, the `Faults` that lose or delay a reply after the charge, and the service). Both are finished.

In `IdempotencyStore.kt`, write `once`: claim the key with `putIfAbsent`, run the work only if you won the claim, and on a hit compare fingerprints and wait for the first result. Run `./gradlew :flow:test --tests 'sfz.enc.l04.IdempotencyStoreTest'` until its five tests pass.
In `ChargeClient.kt`, write `charge`: one key, then a loop that gives every attempt a fresh deadline, retries only the `RETRYABLE` codes with full-jitter backoff, and stops after `maxAttempts`.
Run all 11. The last test charges 30 payments through a network that loses every third first reply. It expects exactly 10 duplicate charges without the key store and none with it.
hints: `putIfAbsent` returns null to exactly one caller, and that caller does the work. Everyone else gets the winner's `Entry` and calls `entry.result.join()`, which waits if the work is still running.
Make the key before the loop. A key made inside it turns every attempt into a new payment, and the lost-reply test checks that the server saw only one key.
Catch `StatusRuntimeException` and look at `e.status.code`. If it isn't in `RETRYABLE`, or this was the last attempt, rethrow `e` itself so the caller sees the real status.
If the slow-reply test takes a whole second, the deadline isn't set: pass `CallOptions.DEFAULT.withDeadlineAfter(...)` to `blockingUnaryCall`.

drill.title: Write the safe retry loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. Write `chargeWithRetries(channel, paymentId, cents)`: one idempotency key, a 200 ms deadline per attempt, at most 4 attempts, retry only `UNAVAILABLE` and `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, with full-jitter backoff starting at 10 ms. Then compare with the answer. Did you make the key before the loop, and did you rethrow the last error?

recap: A remote call has an ending a local call doesn't: no answer, and no way to tell a lost request from a lost reply. Waldo and colleagues argued in 1994 that interfaces must show this, not hide it.

REST names resources with URLs and uses HTTP's methods and status codes; OpenAPI writes the contract down so CI can catch breaking changes. Servers deploy first, so requests must stay backward compatible and responses forward compatible.
Stripe pins each account to a dated API version and converts responses back from the newest shape; since 2024 only two releases a year may break.
gRPC is a Protobuf contract on HTTP/2 streams. It sets no deadline unless you do; a deadline travels as time remaining and follows the request into downstream calls.
A gRPC channel is one long-lived connection, so an L4 balancer pins it to one backend. Balance each stream at L7 (Envoy, a mesh) or in the client (`round_robin` over a headless Service).
Retry only with an idempotency key made once per operation, claimed by the server before the work, and passed on to every service downstream.

quiz.q: Checkout calls payments with a 500 ms deadline. Payments spends 200 ms on its own work, then calls the issuer with grpc-java without setting a deadline. How long can the issuer's handler work before its call is cancelled?
options: 500 ms, the original deadline
About 300 ms: the remaining time travels with the call
As long as it likes: no deadline was set on that call
200 ms
quiz.why: grpc-java hands the remaining deadline of the incoming call to calls made while handling it, and the deadline travels as time remaining. 500 minus 200 leaves about 300 ms. The third option is the default for a call made outside any request context, which is why every top-level call needs a deadline.

quiz.q: Your gRPC fraud service runs 6 pods behind an ordinary Kubernetes ClusterIP Service. Checkout runs 2 pods, each with one long-lived gRPC channel. The autoscaler grows the fraud service to 12 pods. What happens to checkout's traffic?
options: It spreads evenly over the 12 pods within seconds
kube-proxy moves streams from busy pods to the new ones
Each call opens a new connection, so the new pods share the load at once
At most 2 fraud pods serve checkout, until those connections are closed and reopened
quiz.why: kube-proxy balances connections at L4, and each channel has one HTTP/2 connection carrying every call, so 2 channels reach at most 2 pods. New pods get checkout's traffic only after a reconnect. The fixes are a headless Service with client-side `round_robin`, an L7 proxy or mesh, or a server-side maximum connection age.

quiz.q: You add `string currency = 4;` to `ChargeRequest` and deploy the new payment server before the clients. An old client sends a request without field 4. What does the new server see?
options: A parse error, because a field is missing
The gRPC layer rejects the request with INVALID_ARGUMENT
`currency` is the empty string, Protobuf's default, so the server must read it as the old meaning (EUR)
Field 3's value is shifted into field 4
quiz.why: A field missing from the bytes reads as its default, here the empty string, which is what makes a new reader backward compatible with old writers. Nothing fails, so the server code has to decide what an empty currency means. Neither Protobuf nor gRPC checks that every field is present.

quiz.q: A client retries `POST /v1/charges` with the same `Idempotency-Key` and the same body 30 hours after the first attempt, which had succeeded. What can happen at Stripe?
options: Stripe may already have pruned the key, so the retry can create a second charge
Stripe always replays the first response
Stripe rejects the request because the key is too old
Stripe answers 409 Conflict
quiz.why: Stripe keeps keys for at least 24 hours and may prune them after that; a pruned key makes the request new. Retries belong inside the window, which is why clients cap their total retry time. 409 is what a request gets while another one with the same key is still running.

quiz.q: A gRPC call to `Charge` fails with `INVALID_ARGUMENT: amount must be positive`. What should a well-built client do?
options: Retry with backoff, since the server might recover
Retry once with a new idempotency key
Give up at once and report the error: the same request will fail the same way
Switch to another replica and retry there
quiz.why: `INVALID_ARGUMENT` describes the request, not the network or the server's health, so every attempt gets the same answer. Retry `UNAVAILABLE` (didn't get through) and, with a key, `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` (unknown). A new key would not help: it only makes the server forget that this was the same request.

flashcards.front: Which four differences between local and remote calls did Waldo and colleagues name in 1994?
flashcards.back: Latency, memory access (pointers mean nothing elsewhere), partial failure and concurrency. Interfaces should expose them, not hide them.

flashcards.front: What does `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` tell you about a payment?
flashcards.back: Nothing about the outcome. The request or the reply may have been lost, or the server may still be working.

flashcards.front: What deadline does a gRPC call have if you set none?
Why does an L4 load balancer pin gRPC traffic to one backend?
flashcards.back: It picks a backend per TCP connection, and a gRPC channel sends all its calls over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection.

flashcards.front: Where does a gRPC call's real outcome travel?
flashcards.back: In the trailers, as `grpc-status`. The HTTP status is 200 either way.

flashcards.front: How long does Stripe keep idempotency keys?
flashcards.back: At least 24 hours. After that it may prune them, and a retry counts as a new request.

flashcards.front: When does the client make an idempotency key?
flashcards.back: Once per logical operation, before the first attempt. Every retry sends the same key.

terms.plain: Calling a function in another process or machine through a stub that looks like a local call.
The goal of making a remote call look exactly like a local one. Waldo and colleagues argued it can't be done safely.
A YAML or JSON description of an HTTP API: paths, parameters, schemas and status codes. Tools generate clients, docs and checks from it.
The point in time after which a client stops waiting for a call. gRPC sends it as time remaining and passes it on to downstream calls.
One of 17 codes, sent in the trailers, that says how a call ended: OK, UNAVAILABLE, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, INVALID_ARGUMENT and so on.
How a client finds the current addresses of a service's instances: DNS, a registry such as etcd or Consul, or Kubernetes endpoints.
A Kubernetes Service with `clusterIP: None`. DNS returns every pod's IP, so the client can balance across them itself.
A unique ID the client makes once per operation and sends on every attempt, so the server can answer a retry with the first result.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague says: "gRPC is just faster REST, and retries are harmless inside our cluster because the network there is reliable." Explain what is wrong with both halves.
explain_back.answer: gRPC is RPC with a Protobuf contract, one long-lived HTTP/2 connection per channel, deadlines that travel with the call and status codes in trailers. The connection model changes load balancing: an L4 balancer pins all of a channel's calls to one backend, so you need per-stream balancing at L7 or in the client. Browsers also can't call it directly without gRPC-Web or Connect. As for retries, a reliable network still loses replies when a pod is killed, a node fails or a deploy cuts connections, and a slow server looks exactly like a lost reply. After a timeout the client can't know whether the work was done. A retry without an idempotency key, made once per operation and claimed by the server before the work, can charge a card twice, and inside a cluster it happens faster.

deeper.body:
Read Waldo and colleagues' "A Note on Distributed Computing" in full; it is under 15 pages and has aged well. Its target was the 1990s dream of unified objects, but every argument applies to a generated gRPC stub that someone calls in a loop as if it were a local method.

gRPC has two more tools worth knowing. Hedging sends a second copy of a call if the first hasn't answered after a delay, and takes whichever answer comes first: good for cutting tail latency on reads, dangerous on anything with side effects. And xDS lets gRPC clients take their balancing and routing configuration from the same control plane that drives Envoy, so a mesh can run without a sidecar proxy.

GraphQL takes a third path for APIs: one endpoint, a typed schema, and clients that ask for exactly the fields they need. Its answer to versioning is to never break the schema: add fields, mark old ones deprecated, and watch which clients still use them. The Data models track's lesson on GraphQL covers it as a query language.

For the book's framing of services, service discovery and RPC compatibility, see Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 5. The book's point that servers update first, so requests need backward and responses forward compatibility, is the rule this lesson applied to REST, gRPC and Stripe's versions.
